Aminata Diallo is a young woman living in a rented room in a bustling district on the outskirts of Bamako, where the walls are packed earth and the roof is corrugated tin. She works six days a week on a construction crew as the youngest person there and the only woman. Her master mason, Sékou, an older man who lost two fingers to a faulty crane, teases her by calling her la petite comptable because she mentally recalculates load-bearing estimates before lifting a trowel. She is quiet and reserved; she typically responds to teasing with a nod rather than laughter and checks measurements again rather than relying on a first pass.

Her background is shaped by poverty, loss, and financial caution. She learned to double-check calculations from watching her mother lose a market stall to a miscalculated loan. Her mother died when Aminata was twelve. She also remembers that her father once sold his tools to pay for a funeral and never worked with a trowel again. She has counted everything ever since: bricks, rice costs, weeks until an accounting exam. She keeps a small notebook tucked inside her shirt with figures and dates, and she hides an emergency fund under the loosest floorboard near her mattress. She adds the same amount each month, does not touch it, and does not count it in daylight. She values careful counting, self-verification, and financial caution, and she prefers to rely on what she has counted herself.

Aminata is enrolled in accounting exam preparation at a community center and is saving for an accounting course. She studies at night by the light of a kerosene lamp after long workdays, even when her eyes burn. She cannot afford bus fare both ways to the community center, so she walks. She is disciplined and self-controlled, never asks for an advance on her wage, and keeps personal plans private. She is also saving for a proper room with running water so her younger sister can live with her and attend school. She does not speak of this plan aloud because she believes such plans can be borrowed against. Her coworkers respect her silence, precision, and reliability. It is nearly dusk. Aminata is walking back from the community center after her accounting exam prep. She passes a small tea stall. A young man she has seen several times at the center, and who often smiles at her, raises his hand and offers to buy her a glass of sweet tea. The stall is warm and lit, and a vendor is pouring another glass. The man is waiting for her answer. Aminata is tired, her soles ache, and she still has a long walk ahead to her room.

Aminata’s legs ache from hauling cement and from the walk to the center. She is thirsty and has not eaten since early afternoon. Her mind remains heavy with the accounting problems from the prep session. The warm lamp in the stall reminds her of studying by her own kerosene lamp late at night. The young man’s smile recalls a boy at the market who smiled before asking her to carry his goods for free. The scent of sweet tea reminds her of the glass her mother bought her on market days before she died. She knows the young man only by sight from the exam prep class at the community center. He has smiled at her before, but they have never spoken, and she has no other connection to him. She has never accepted a gift or favor from a man she does not know well. When offered a free drink by a stall owner once, she politely declined and bought her own. She habitually avoids stopping on her walk home because delays mean arriving after dark.
